slides.title: How I Build
slides.subtitle: A standard product development lifecycle — adapted so one person can run every phase.
slides.takeaway: After the pilot you don't start over — you loop back to Architect and go deeper. That's a living system, not a one-time build.

notes.intent: Frame the process as the lifecycle everyone knows, then land the real insight: after a pilot it loops back to Architect, not the start.
notes.summary:
• Say it plainly: this is the same development lifecycle everyone here knows — Validate through Feedback.
• Click through the phases as you talk; don't read all six, hit the arc.
• Land the loop on the last click: when you hit Feedback, the arc draws back to Architect — 'you don't start over, you go back to plan the updates and go deeper.'
• That return, with no endpoint, is what makes it a living system. Release happens when feedback's clean and stakeholders align — and even that can drop back into the loop.
• The other half of the point: normally each phase leans on a different team. I run the whole loop solo.
notes.bridge: Running this whole loop alone only works because of how I use AI. Here's the toolkit.

slides.title: The AI Behind It
slides.subtitle: Walk the chain — each tool takes the last one's output as its input.
slides.takeaway: One developer can run the whole lifecycle when each phase has the right AI tool.

notes.intent: Make AI concrete — walk the carousel one tool at a time so the room sees each phase's tool AND the artifact it hands to the next.
notes.summary:
• Step through with the arrows — one tool per view, input on the left, output on the right.
• The whole point: each tool's output becomes the next tool's input. Say that as you advance.
• Immerse — Claude Projects: the whole problem in; research agents study prior art → a context report.
• Architect — grill-me interviews me into a design spec (the next slide is the payoff), then writing-plans breaks that spec into parallel lanes → an implementation plan.
• Prototype — dispatching-parallel-agents: a controller scopes each subagent's context and permissions, then verifies every result against the plan's tests → a working prototype.
• Feedback — readme-kit logs every change and maps the version so anything can be reverted → then it loops back to Architect.
• Say it out loud: Validate and Deploy have no tool — deciding it's worth building, and shipping it, are still me. AI doesn't pick the problem.
• Don't linger on any one tool; the story is the handoff chain.
notes.bridge: Of all of these, the one people ask me about most is grill-me. Let me show you what it actually does.

tools.desc: Discusses the problem and the steps to a solution, and deploys research agents to study how others have solved it.
Interviews me into an airtight spec — surfaces blind spots and presents alternative solutions with their tradeoffs.
Breaks the design spec into parallel development lanes.

Delegates each task to a specialized agent with a focused scope. The controller gives each only the context it needs and scopes its permissions so lanes don't conflict — then verifies every result against the predefined tests.
After every update, documents the changes in a standard format and maps the version bump — so breaking changes can be tracked and reverted if needed.

slides.title: Inside grill-me
slides.subtitle: How a rough idea becomes a spec I can build from.
slides.takeaway: It won't let me hand-wave — every assumption gets a decision before a line of code is written.

notes.intent: Make grill-me concrete and stealable — show it catching a definitional decision before any code.
notes.summary:
• Frame it: I start vague, and grill-me won't let me stay vague.
• The length is the point — it asks 20+ questions, one at a time. The badge stands in for that; don't read a transcript.
• Walk the one exchange: it asked whether 'hours per engineer' should include admin and out-of-office. That's a definition that would've made every chart wrong.
• Land the SPEC: Productive Hours = logged − admin − OOO, decided before building anything.
• This is the part people can steal tomorrow — flag it for Q&A.
notes.bridge: So that's how I build. Now — when do I point all this at a problem? When I see these signals.

content.lead: Before I write any code, grill-me interviews me about the idea — one question at a time, until every assumption has a decision.
content.askLabel: THE ROUGH IDEA I WALKED IN WITH
content.ask: I've got a pile of LiquidPlanner timesheet data. What KPIs can we pull out of it, and what should I build to view it?

turns.text: Should "hours per engineer" include admin time and out-of-office — or only project work?
…only productive work. Exclude admin and out-of-office, and label it clearly.

content.outcome: → SPEC: "Productive Hours = logged − admin − out-of-office" — defined before a single chart was built.
content.footnote: One representative exchange from a much longer session. The full output is an implementation plan handed straight to the build step.

slides.title: The Signals
slides.subtitle: The patterns that say a workflow is ready to become a tool.
slides.takeaway: We're not short on engineering talent — we're short on tools built for the way we actually work.

notes.intent: Give the audience a checklist they recognize, so the demos land as answers to a problem they have too.

slides.title: VicFlex Bracket Filter
slides.subtitle: A high-frequency lookup, turned into a self-service tool — live.
slides.takeaway: Automating the decision you make 40 times beats optimizing the one you make once.

notes.intent: Land VicFlex fast — one setup line plus two relatable pairs set up a quick live demo. Tell the Brian/intern story aloud.
notes.summary:
• Tell the Brian/intern story out loud — it lands better than bullets, especially with Brian in the room: the repeated lookup pulling him into SolidWorks, his interns' database, the shopping-style filter.
• On screen: one setup line + the two Signal→Target pairs (the reusable model).
• Two pairs only — tribal knowledge becomes queryable, the bottleneck becomes self-service.
• Get to LAUNCH fast: pick known components, instant compatible configs against the D-value threshold (~5 min). Screenshots ready as backup.
notes.bridge: So what did giving that time back actually look like?

origin.setup: The modular VicFlex bracket line has tons of possible configurations — and every compatibility question kept landing on engineering.

signal.v: Compatibility logic stayed locked with project and application engineers.

target.v: Navigate the database from known or desired parts — the knowledge is now queryable by anyone.

signal.v: To recommend a config, Sales had to reach out to engineering to confirm compatibility.

target.v: Sales answers compatibility themselves, instantly — no round-trip.

slides.title: VicFlex: Hours Recovered
slides.subtitle: What self-service gives back to engineering.
slides.takeaway: Three hours a week, back for NPD — every week, all year.

notes.intent: Put a real, measured number on the VicFlex win and make it human.
notes.summary:
• Human first: 3 hours a week, every week — then let the curve climb to 156.
• Measured, not modeled: 2 requests/week × 1.5 hrs × 52 = 156 hours.
• Now it's self-service, so the residual is basically zero — the recovered area is the whole chart.
• Make it Brian, not 'engineering' — that's NPD time back in his week.
• The right column is the derivation; let the room follow the arithmetic.
notes.bridge: Now here's the same process applied to a much more complex product.

points.label: The lookup
points.text: ~2 requests a week, ~1.5 hours each in SolidWorks.

points.label: With the tool
points.text: Sales self-serves → about zero. Nearly all of it recovered.

points.label: Human scale
points.text: ~3 hours a week back in Brian's week, for NPD.

slides.title: Vortex Project Builder
slides.subtitle: Four scattered sources, replaced by one validated tool — live.
slides.takeaway: One stop: configure, validate, price, and export — same inputs, same output, every engineer.

notes.intent: Land the one-stop-shop: the builder packages four old sources into one validated flow. Keep the source docs openable as live backup.
notes.summary:
• One line on the product: a hybrid suppression system — powerful, painful to configure.
• The four chips are the old way — open one or two live (the Estimator with its hand calcs is the vivid one), let the rest just sit there making the point. No single source of truth, so quality depended on who did it.
• Two pairs: hand calcs become a transparent calc engine; four sources become one flow.
• Maturity line, spoken: I didn't just digitize the sheets — I restructured the method into one model, then encoded it once.
• Launch live: load a preset, define two zones, trigger a warning on purpose, export the BOM (~7 min). Screenshots ready as backup.
notes.bridge: And the value of that doesn't stay flat — it grows with the project.

origin.setup: One of our most capable products — a hybrid suppression system, powerful in the field but painful to configure. A single design used to mean four disconnected sources, with no single source of truth:

signal.v: Project complexity scaled the design-calculation complexity — all worked out by hand.

target.v: Handles the math and shows its work, so the logic stays validated — no more hand calcs.

signal.v: One estimate meant juggling async files — price list, manual, codes — plus hand calcs and coordination across Sales, Apps Eng & Customer Care.

target.v: Price list & partcodes build an accurate BOM as you configure — then quote, export for Applications, and hand to Customer Care from one flow.

slides.title: Vortex: Effort vs. Complexity
slides.subtitle: Why the tool's value grows with the project.
slides.takeaway: The more complex the project, the wider the gap — and the more the tool saves.

notes.intent: Show the shape of the savings honestly — assert the shape, not exact numbers — and let the divergence be the argument.
notes.summary:
• Be upfront: VicFlex I can measure to the hour; this one's a model. I'm asserting the shape, not numbers — there are no ticks on the axes.
• Read the right column: base effort, then the old method goes exponential (every added zone or enclosure compounds, rework restarts), while the builder stays near-flat (complexity = clicks, not effort).
• The widening gap is the point — even worst case the old way scales numerically worse.
• The line to land: effort stays flat as complexity grows.
notes.bridge: So if any of this sounds like your day to day — let's take one and think it through together.

points.label: Base effort
points.text: Every project starts with the same baseline estimate work — the y-intercept.

points.label: Old method → exponential
points.text: Hand calcs, async files, and coordination across departments — each added zone or enclosure compounds across every layer, and any rework meant starting from scratch.

points.label: Vortex Builder → near-flat
points.text: Same baseline; each added zone is just a few more clicks. Complexity drives clicks, not effort.

points.label: The gap
points.text: Even worst-case, the divergence compounds — the old way scales numerically worse.

slides.title: Is This Your Workflow?
slides.subtitle: What to look for — and how to approach it.
slides.takeaway: Make the correct way the easy way.

notes.intent: Recap the takeaways — the signals and the process — then open the room to think one through live. No self-promotion.
notes.summary:
• Recap, turned on them: the signals to watch for in your own work, and the process — simplified — to approach them.
• Read a couple signals slowly; let people picture their own workflow.
• Open question: 'What's one thing you've always wanted to automate?' Take ONE and walk it down the seven steps OUT LOUD with the room — this is a verbal think-through, NOT a live grill-me session. Don't run the tool live.
• You don't have to solve it — just model the thinking, and end branches with 'and that's where grill-me takes over.'
• Have a backup workflow in your pocket in case the room's quiet. Time-box to one example, then open broader Q&A.
• Land the line last: 'Make the correct way the easy way.'
notes.bridge: So — what's one you'd want to take on? Let's pick one and walk it. (open Q&A)
